value.overview: The Eurasian Collared-Dove is a pale, adaptable dove recognized by its narrow black-and-white collar and repeated three-part coo. Native to Europe, North Africa, and much of Asia, it has expanded widely through introductions and natural colonization, including the Caribbean, North America, and parts of Central America. It commonly lives around farms, towns, suburbs, gardens, and other open landscapes, where it often feeds on the ground and rests on buildings, wires, and trees.
value.classification: The Eurasian Collared-Dove belongs to the order Columbiformes and family Columbidae, the pigeon and dove family. Its scientific name is Streptopelia decaocto.
value.identification: This is a medium-large dove, about 30 to 33 centimeters long, with a slim body, small head, long square-tipped tail, and pale gray-buff to pinkish-gray plumage. Adults have a distinct black crescent or partial collar on the back and sides of the neck, edged in white. The wingtips are darker than the back, while the tail is mostly white below with darker outer edges. The voice is a clear, rhythmic three-note coo, often rendered as “coo-COO-coo.”
value.rangeHabitat: The species is native across a broad zone from Europe and North Africa through the Middle East and Asia, and it has become established in many introduced regions. In Costa Rica it is an introduced, uncommon, and locally recorded bird rather than a widespread native species. Verified records include observations around developed coastal areas such as Jacó in Puntarenas. It is most likely to occur in open, human-modified habitats, including towns, farms, gardens, roadsides, and other lowland landscapes, rather than extensive forest.
value.migrationStatus: Generally sedentary or locally dispersive. In Costa Rica, available records indicate an introduced or vagrant occurrence without evidence of regular long-distance migration or a well-defined seasonal passage.
value.breeding: Eurasian Collared-Doves can breed in many months where conditions are favorable, with timing influenced by food supply and weather. The nest is usually a flimsy platform of twigs placed in trees, shrubs, on buildings, or on other structures. A typical clutch contains two white eggs, and both adults share incubation and care of the young. The species may raise several broods in a year. Regular breeding in Costa Rica has not been reliably established from the available information.
value.dietFeeding: The diet consists mainly of seeds and grains, supplemented by fruits, buds, and other plant material. Around farms and settlements, the birds commonly feed on spilled grain, birdseed, and food beneath trees or feeders. They usually forage by walking on open ground, often alone, in pairs, or in small groups. Their tolerance of people and ability to exploit cultivated landscapes help explain their success in towns, agricultural areas, and other disturbed habitats.
value.behavior: Eurasian Collared-Doves are often seen perched conspicuously on wires, rooftops, poles, and bare branches. They frequently occur in pairs and defend territories with repeated calling, although nonbreeding birds may gather in loose flocks where food is abundant. The flight is strong and direct, with occasional gliding. Courtship includes bowing displays, vocalizing, and aerial flights. The species is generally wary but adapts readily to human presence and urban environments.

conservation.populationTrend: Increasing globally, with continuing expansion in several introduced regions, although local populations may fluctuate.
